posts.first: I rode a lot of horses before her, and every one of them had a way of keeping me honest. She just does it with better posture. The ribbon is hanging above her stall right now. I'd say she earned it, and she'd say I'm welcome.

posts.theme: the horse budget vs. the spouse
posts.quote: Our hay budget and our household budget haven't been in the same room since March. It's how we stay married.
posts.first: My husband still thinks the second budget is a hobby. It has its own spreadsheet and a folder labeled Misc. In my defense, the folder is mostly receipts for hay and one small mineral block. He opened it once, looked at the total, and closed it. We had pasta for dinner and watched a movie.

posts.caption: I get to the barn at ten to five most mornings, and my gray gelding is almost always already awake, standing at the front of his stall with his ears forward. I braid his mane in the winter because it keeps the hay out. I hum while I do it. Last week a boarder asked what song that was and I realized I couldn't say. I've hummed it so long it came with the barn. He was perfectly still the whole time, as he always is.
posts.first: I started braiding his mane when he was twelve and I was somewhere in my forties. Now he's twenty-six and my hands don't work as fast as they used to. He stands just as still as ever, though, and never once rushes me. I think that's his way of saying thank you.

posts.caption: The vet's truck pulled in at 8:20, five minutes early, which is how I knew it was going to be a long morning. Red watched him unload from the barn door like a night guard reviewing a visitor log. He said it would be quick. She lifted one front hoof about an inch off the ground and left it there. He did the whole exam with great politeness and a small amount of sweat. When he finished, she put the hoof down and turned her back. I paid by check. Nobody said much on the drive out.
posts.first: Red has opinions about the vet and she shares them without ever raising her voice or moving her feet. We have a deal. I hold the lead rope and nod, and she keeps her hoof where it is. The vet gets the ground and she gets the last word.

posts.caption: Something moved in the hedge by the barn at 6:15 and every horse on the property had an opinion. The gelding bolted to the far end of his run. The mare in the corner stall started pacing, and two of the ponies stared at it like it owed them money. Mine kept eating. She flicked an ear and chewed for another minute. It turned out to be a very surprised wild turkey, and mine looked at it exactly once. She's been the calm one in this barn for nine years.
posts.first: I've taken her out in a lot of weather and she's never made a fuss about any of it. She treats the world like a very slow television show. When she's worried, I'm worried, and when she's bored, I know it's fine. It makes feeding time easier.
